question: According to the 2025 budget, by what year does India aim to reduce central government debt to 50% of GDP?
solution_text:
The correct answer is March 2031.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the Union Budget 2025-26, the Finance Ministry announced a new medium-term fiscal consolidation roadmap shifting India's fiscal anchor from a pure annual fiscal-deficit target to managing the central government's debt-to-GDP ratio, aiming to bring it down to approximately 50% of GDP by around Financial Year 2030-31 (i.e., by March 2031).

• This roadmap reflects a broader, more sustainable approach to fiscal management, moving away from a rigid year-on-year fiscal deficit number toward a longer-term framework focused on overall public debt sustainability, in line with recommendations from bodies like the N.K. Singh-led FRBM Review Committee (2017), which had earlier proposed debt-based fiscal anchors.

• As of the time of the Budget announcement, India's central government debt-to-GDP ratio stood at roughly 57-58%, with the government targeting a gradual reduction of about 1 percentage point per year over the following several years to reach the 50% target by around FY31.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The FRBM Act (Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2003) has historically governed India's fiscal deficit and debt targets, and has been amended multiple times to adjust deficit/debt targets in response to changing economic circumstances (e.g., the COVID-19 pandemic).

• Shifting the fiscal anchor to a debt-to-GDP target is intended to give the government greater flexibility during periods of economic stress (allowing higher deficits temporarily) while maintaining a credible long-term path toward fiscal sustainability.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 (March 2028): This is an earlier date than the government's actual announced target year for reaching the 50% debt-to-GDP ratio.

• Option 2 (March 2029): Also earlier than the correct target year announced in the Budget 2025-26 roadmap.

• Option 3 (March 2030): Close to, but not the precise, officially stated target year — the roadmap specifically points to around FY31 (ending March 2031), not FY30.

question: Which sector saw the entry of new private Indian and foreign banks due to post-1991 reforms?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Banking.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• As part of India's post-1991 economic reforms, the banking sector was significantly liberalised — the Narasimham Committee (1991 and 1998) recommended reforms including allowing the entry of new private sector banks and easing restrictions on foreign banks, ending decades of an almost entirely public-sector-dominated banking landscape (which had prevailed since the bank nationalisations of 1969 and 1980).

• Following these reforms, the RBI granted licences to a new generation of private banks in the 1990s — including institutions like ICICI Bank, HDFC Bank, Axis Bank (originally UTI Bank), and IndusInd Bank — marking a major structural shift toward greater competition, efficiency and customer service standards in Indian banking.

• Foreign banks were also permitted greater market access, and later rounds of licensing (e.g., in 2003-04 and again in 2013-14, which led to the licensing of Kotak Mahindra Bank, Yes Bank, IDFC First Bank, and Bandhan Bank) continued this trend of opening up the banking sector to new private players.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Narasimham Committee reports also recommended reducing the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) and Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR), introducing prudential norms for asset classification (NPA recognition), and strengthening bank supervision — all aimed at making Indian banking more efficient, competitive and aligned with international standards.

• Prior to 1991, Indian banking was dominated by public sector banks (PSBs) following nationalisation, with very limited scope for private or foreign bank participation.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 (Textile): While the textile sector saw various policy reforms and was traditionally important to India's economy and exports, it was not the sector specifically associated with the entry of new private/foreign banks under 1991 reforms.

• Option 3 (Mining): The mining sector saw its own separate reforms over time (e.g., relating to coal sector liberalisation, mostly in later years), but is unrelated to the specific banking-sector liberalisation described in the question.

• Option 4 (Railways): Indian Railways remained, and largely remains, a government-run entity; it was not a sector that saw private/foreign bank entry as part of the 1991 reforms.

question: The New Economic Policy 1991 aimed to reduce fiscal deficit to what medium-term percentage of GDP?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 3-4%.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• India's New Economic Policy of 1991, launched amid a severe balance-of-payments crisis, set a medium-term fiscal consolidation target of bringing the fiscal deficit down to around 3-4% of GDP, as India's fiscal deficit had ballooned to a crisis level of roughly 8% of GDP in 1990-91, contributing significantly to the macroeconomic instability that triggered the reforms.

• This target reflected international best-practice thinking at the time on sustainable fiscal management, and became a recurring benchmark referenced in subsequent Indian fiscal policy discussions, including later being formalised (with some variation) through the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003, which originally targeted a fiscal deficit of 3% of GDP.

• Reducing the fiscal deficit was one of several core pillars of the 1991 stabilisation-cum-structural-reform programme, alongside devaluation of the rupee, reduction of import tariffs, industrial delicensing, and opening up to foreign investment.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• India's fiscal deficit had reached approximately 8.2% of GDP in 1990-91, a key factor (alongside dwindling foreign exchange reserves, which fell to barely a few weeks of import cover) that forced India to approach the IMF and World Bank for emergency assistance and undertake structural reforms in 1991.

• The FRBM Act, 2003 later institutionalised fiscal deficit and debt targets into law, though the specific targets have been revised multiple times since (including amendments in 2018 and during the COVID-19 period) to reflect changing economic conditions.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 (10.00%): This figure is far higher than the fiscal deficit target sought — indeed, higher even than the crisis-level deficit India was trying to reduce from (around 8%) in 1991.

• Option 2 (7.0%): Still higher than the specific medium-term target of 3-4% of GDP set as part of the 1991 reform programme.

• Option 4 (8-9%): This range approximates India's pre-reform crisis-level fiscal deficit (the problem the reforms sought to fix), not the medium-term target the reforms aimed to achieve.

question: What major 2025 reform now ranks Indian states on investment friendliness for EoDB?

• The goal of such rankings is to create healthy competition among states to improve their regulatory environment, infrastructure, and ease of setting up and operating businesses, thereby attracting greater domestic and foreign investment.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Earlier state competitiveness frameworks in India have included the DPIIT's Ease of Doing Business rankings/BRAP (last major iteration for 2022) and NITI Aayog's various sectoral indices (like the SDG India Index), reflecting a broader trend of using rankings/indices to drive state-level policy reform.

• Option 2 (State SDG Index): The SDG India Index, published by NITI Aayog, tracks states' progress on the UN Sustainable Development Goals — a broader development metric, not specifically an investment-friendliness/EoDB ranking tool.

question: Which act provides the legislative framework for the use of electronic evidence in courts from July 2024?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), 2023, which came into force on 1 July 2024, replaced the colonial-era Indian Evidence Act, 1872, and provides the updated legislative framework governing the admissibility, presentation and evaluation of evidence — including electronic and digital evidence — in Indian courts.

• The BSA explicitly expands and modernises provisions relating to electronic records, treating properly authenticated digital/electronic evidence (emails, digital documents, server logs, electronic communications, etc.) as admissible primary evidence, reflecting the increasing role of digital documentation and communication in contemporary legal proceedings.

• This modernisation is part of the broader criminal law reform package that also introduced the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023 (replacing the IPC) and the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 (replacing the CrPC), all effective from 1 July 2024.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The BSA's enhanced provisions for electronic evidence are seen as particularly significant given the rapid growth of cybercrime, digital communications, and forensic technology use in modern criminal investigations and trials.

• The overall philosophy behind the three new criminal law statutes, as emphasised by the government, is to modernise India's criminal justice system with a victim-centric, technology-enabled, and time-bound approach, moving away from colonial-era legal frameworks.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 (Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita): This is the substantive criminal law (replacing the Indian Penal Code, 1860), defining offences and punishments, not the law governing rules of evidence.

• Option 2 (Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita): This is the procedural law (replacing the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973), governing investigation, arrest, trial and procedural aspects of criminal cases, not the specific law on evidence.

• Option 4 (Uniform Civil Code): The UCC is a proposed/directive constitutional goal (Article 44) for a common set of personal laws across religious communities in matters like marriage, divorce and inheritance — it is unrelated to rules of evidence and has not been enacted as a central law as of the relevant period.

question: As per 2025, the UDAN scheme seeks to expand connectivity to how many new destinations?

The correct answer is 120.

question: Acceleration due to gravity on Earth is approximately?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 9.8 m/s².

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The standard acceleration due to gravity (g) on the surface of the Earth is approximately 9.8 m/s² (more precisely, 9.80665 m/s² by international standard convention), representing the rate at which an object accelerates when falling freely under Earth's gravitational pull, ignoring air resistance.

• This value arises from Newton's law of universal gravitation, F = GMm/r², where G is the universal gravitational constant, M is Earth's mass, and r is the distance from Earth's centre (approximately Earth's radius at the surface).

• The value of "g" varies slightly with latitude and altitude — it is marginally higher at the poles (due to Earth's oblate shape and slightly shorter distance to the centre) and lower at the equator and at higher altitudes, but 9.8 m/s² is the standard approximate value used in most physics calculations.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Universal Gravitational Constant (G), a distinct value from "g", is approximately 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg², used in Newton's law of gravitation to calculate gravitational force between any two masses — this is often confused with "g" in exam questions, as reflected in Option 3 here (6.67, which resembles G's numerical coefficient, not g's value).

• The concept of "g" is fundamental to numerous physics calculations, including projectile motion, weight (W = mg), and orbital mechanics.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 (4.9 m/s²): This is exactly half of the correct value of g and does not correspond to Earth's actual gravitational acceleration.

• Option 3 (6.67 m/s²): This numerically resembles the gravitational constant (G ≈ 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹), not the acceleration due to gravity (g), and is a common point of confusion between these two distinct physical quantities.

• Option 4 (10.6 m/s²): This value is higher than Earth's actual gravitational acceleration and does not correspond to any standard physical constant relevant to this context.

question: Which festival is celebrated by tying a 'rakhi' for symbolizing sibling love?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Raksha Bandhan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Raksha Bandhan ("bond of protection") is a Hindu festival celebrating the bond between brothers and sisters, during which sisters tie a sacred thread called a "rakhi" around their brothers' wrists, symbolising love, protection and the sibling bond, while brothers traditionally offer gifts and pledge to protect their sisters.

• It is celebrated on the full moon day (Purnima) of the Hindu month of Shravana (typically falling in August), and is observed widely across North and Central India, with regional variations in customs and associated names (e.g., "Rakhi Purnima").

• The festival has also acquired broader symbolic meanings over time, sometimes extended to express protective bonds beyond biological siblings, and is one of India's most widely recognised familial festivals.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Raksha Bandhan coincides, in some regions, with other festivals observed on the same Shravana Purnima day, such as "Kajari Purnima" and, in coastal Maharashtra/Konkan, "Narali Purnima" (coconut festival, marking the fishing community's post-monsoon return to the sea).

• The rakhi thread itself can range from simple cotton threads to elaborately decorated ones, and the festival has also inspired symbolic gestures of unity, such as tying rakhis to trees for environmental awareness campaigns.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 (Pongal): A Tamil Nadu harvest festival, dedicated to the Sun God, unrelated to the sibling-bond rakhi tradition.

question: In which festival are diyas and fireworks important due to the return of Lord Rama to Ayodhya, but also the peak business season for sweets and gifts?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Diwali.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Diwali (Deepavali), the "Festival of Lights", commemorates the return of Lord Rama, Sita and Lakshmana to Ayodhya after 14 years of exile and after Rama's victory over the demon king Ravana, as narrated in the Ramayana; the citizens of Ayodhya are said to have lit rows of diyas (oil lamps) to welcome them home, a tradition continued today through lighting diyas and, in modern times, fireworks.

• Diwali is also India's most significant commercial and shopping festival, marking the peak business season for sweets, gifts, new clothes, jewellery, electronics, and home goods, with businesses and markets seeing a major surge in sales in the lead-up to the festival.

• The festival is celebrated over five days, including Dhanteras, Naraka Chaturdashi (Choti Diwali), Lakshmi Puja (main Diwali day), Govardhan Puja, and Bhai Dooj, with worship of Goddess Lakshmi (wealth) and Lord Ganesha central to the main day's celebrations.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Diwali is celebrated not only by Hindus but also holds significance for Jains (commemorating Lord Mahavira's nirvana), Sikhs (commemorating the release of Guru Hargobind Ji, and the founding of the Golden Temple), and Buddhists in some traditions, making it a genuinely pan-religious festival in parts of India.

• Diwali has been increasingly recognised internationally, with celebrations and even official observances (e.g., a designated holiday) in several countries with significant Indian diaspora populations.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 2 (Eid): An Islamic festival, marking the end of Ramadan (Eid-ul-Fitr) or commemorating the willingness of Ibrahim to sacrifice his son (Eid-ul-Adha) — unrelated to the Rama-Ayodhya narrative or the diya/fireworks tradition specific to Diwali.

• Option 3 (Holi): The Hindu "Festival of Colours", celebrating the arrival of spring and the triumph of good (Prahlada) over evil (Holika), involving colour-throwing rather than diyas/fireworks and the Rama-Ayodhya story.

• Option 4 (Christmas): A Christian festival celebrating the birth of Jesus Christ, unrelated to the Ramayana narrative described in the question.

question: Which city was ranked as the most polluted in the world in the World Air Quality Report 2025?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Loni.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• According to the World Air Quality Report 2025, published by the Swiss air-quality monitoring organisation IQAir, Loni, a town in the Ghaziabad district of Uttar Pradesh (part of the National Capital Region, near Delhi), was ranked as the most polluted city in the world, based on average PM2.5 concentration levels recorded through the year.

• The report also found that India was among the countries with the highest concentration of polluted cities globally, and separately noted that Pakistan ranked as the most polluted country overall for 2025 in terms of average national PM2.5 levels.

• Loni's extreme pollution levels have been widely reported as symptomatic of the broader air quality crisis in the Indo-Gangetic Plain/National Capital Region, driven by factors such as vehicular emissions, industrial activity, construction dust, and seasonal agricultural stubble burning.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• PM2.5 refers to fine particulate matter with a diameter of 2.5 micrometres or smaller, which can penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream, posing serious health risks including respiratory and cardiovascular disease; the WHO's air quality guideline for annual PM2.5 exposure is a small fraction of the levels recorded in cities like Loni.

• Several Indian cities have consistently featured among the world's most polluted in recent years' IQAir reports, spurring government initiatives like the National Clean Air Programme (NCAP), aimed at reducing particulate pollution across identified non-attainment cities.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 (Beijing): Once notorious for severe air pollution, Beijing's air quality has improved significantly in recent years due to sustained government pollution-control measures, and it did not top the 2025 rankings.

• Option 2 (Delhi): While Delhi continues to face severe air pollution and frequently ranks among the world's most polluted capital cities, it was not the single most polluted city overall in the 2025 report — that distinction went to nearby Loni.

• Option 3 (Lahore): A major Pakistani city that also suffers from severe air pollution (especially seasonal smog), and while Pakistan was ranked the most polluted country overall, Lahore specifically was not identified as the single most polluted city in the 2025 report.

question: What is the weight of the metal ball used in the shot-put event for male athletes?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 7.26 kg.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the athletics event of Shot Put, the official metal ball (shot) used in men's/male senior international competitions (as per World Athletics rules) weighs 7.26 kg (equivalent to 16 pounds).

• For women's senior competitions, the shot put ball weighs 4 kg, reflecting the different weight standards set for men's and women's events across track and field competitions.

• Shot put involves athletes "putting" (pushing, not throwing) the heavy spherical ball as far as possible from a marked circle, using a technique that generates power primarily from the legs, hips and shoulder in a fluid pushing motion, rather than an overhand throw.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The shot put ball must be made of solid iron, brass, or any metal not softer than brass, and must meet precise specifications for both weight and diameter as set by World Athletics rules.

• Weight categories for various throwing equipment differ by age/category in athletics — for instance, junior and youth categories use lighter implements (e.g., 6 kg, 5 kg, or 4 kg shots) depending on age group, while the 7.26 kg standard applies specifically to senior men's competitions.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 (8.84 kg): This is heavier than the standard men's shot put weight and does not correspond to official World Athletics specifications.

• Option 2 (6.84 kg): Close to, but not the precise, official weight of 7.26 kg specified for men's senior shot put competitions.

• Option 4 (8.26 kg): Also does not match the official men's shot put weight of 7.26 kg as set by World Athletics rules.

question: Who was the first woman from Rajasthan to be arrested during the Indian freedom movement?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Anjana Devi.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Anjana Devi Chaudhary is widely recognised as the first woman from Rajasthan to be arrested for her participation in the Indian freedom movement, reflecting the active, though often lesser-documented, involvement of Rajasthani women in India's independence struggle.

• Rajasthan's contribution to the freedom movement included resistance against both British colonial rule and, in various princely states, against local autocratic rulers, with numerous local movements and satyagrahas taking place across the region's princely states (such as Jaipur, Jodhpur, Bikaner, and others) during the early-to-mid 20th century.

• Women's participation in Rajasthan's freedom struggle, though historically under-recognised compared to more widely known national figures, forms an important part of the broader history of women's contributions to India's independence movement across the country.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other notable women associated with Rajasthan's socio-political history include social reformers and freedom-movement participants whose contributions are increasingly being documented and recognised in regional historical scholarship and state-level competitive exam syllabi.

• Rajasthan's princely states saw numerous Praja Mandal movements (people's movements demanding responsible government within princely states) during the freedom struggle, in which women played active, if often under-recorded, supporting and participatory roles.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 2 (Nagendra Bala): Not specifically recognised as the first woman from Rajasthan to be arrested in the freedom movement in standard historical/exam references.

• Option 3 (Rama Devi): A name associated with freedom movement activism in parts of India (including a notable Rama Devi associated with Odisha's freedom struggle), but not specifically identified as the first woman from Rajasthan to be arrested.

• Option 4 (Bhikaji Cama): A prominent Parsi freedom fighter from Bombay (Maharashtra), renowned for unfurling an early version of the Indian flag at the International Socialist Congress in Stuttgart, Germany (1907) — not from Rajasthan, and unrelated to this specific fact about Rajasthan's freedom movement history.
